title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations and ordered maintenance workflows. Operational deployment requires evidence that model outputs will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to networks. Recent surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, yet reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited.

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design frozen before data collection (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixes generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gate policy, and analysis; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic Batfish‑style validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) interpretation of this degenerate null in terms of ceiling effects traceable in the archived artifacts; and (5) concrete artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps work spans intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, log/RCA, and early agentic automation proposals. Surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1],[2],[5].

Generate–validate–repair architectures have been proposed across domains (NetOps, program repair, DevOps) as a practical path to safer automatic changes; prototype systems and controlled experiments in adjacent domains report promising improvements under specific datasets and validators (for example, program‑repair agents and DevOps runbook safety evaluations) rather than universal guarantees [6],[3]. This literature motivates paired, construct‑valid evaluations that isolate validator effects from model sampling variance.

Methodological gaps. Two gaps motivate our paired design. First, pipeline comparisons that allow different first‑pass model draws per arm confound validator effects with model sampling variance. Second, many existing benchmarks emphasize QA/relevance or log tasks but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. Our shared_initial_candidate experiment isolates the validator/gate effect on identical initial generations and therefore directly addresses the first gap.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1 and fixed the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate, model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1), deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy, repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1), deterministic task selection (task_count = 200 paired intents), and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). These parameters were frozen prior to observing outputs and are archived in the execution manifest.

Generation semantics and sampling. The executed generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent. Thus the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on the identical first‑pass candidate and does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance. The adapter produced one sampled generation per pair (shared_initial_generation stage count = 200).

Model configuration note (explicit). The run used temperature = null as recorded in the archived model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json); null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic model sampling (it does not imply temperature=0), and the adapter does not guarantee deterministic sampling. The experiment therefore makes no claim of deterministic model sampling; it produced exactly one sampled generation per pair that was reused under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Task bank and deterministic sampling. The deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced intent→configuration items containing explicit workflow_policies and required_sequence constraints (sequence ordering, protected interfaces, minimum_up and final_group rules). The preregistered sampler selected 200 paired intents using the adapter's deterministic index rule; selection is fixed and outcome‑independent. Per‑task difficulty metadata (labels such as "very_hard" and "extreme") were recorded in the archived task manifest.

Interventions, gating, and scoring. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate without gating. Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the deterministic gate applied a preregistered accept/reject rule and, on violations, allowed up to one automated repair attempt. The primary outcome was a binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation after validation. Scoring used the full_intent_constraint_validation rule set; validator traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, final_state snapshots, and violation codes.

Confirmatory analysis (frozen). The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 comparing unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs. The 2×2 paired contingency reports discordant pair counts n10 (guarded_only) and n01 (baseline_only), an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent p‑value, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and a single‑retry rule for infrastructure errors were preregistered; no retriable infrastructure failures occurred in this run.

Implementation and archival hygiene. All shared initial generations, per‑episode responses, validator traces, and analysis outputs were recorded during execution and are archived in the evidence bundle. Deterministic reconciliation and provider call audits were executed to confirm accounting and sample provenance.

Every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; the exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These per‑episode diagnostics indicate that the generated commands satisfied the encoded sequencing and precondition checks for the sampled tasks.

sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the selected synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; therefore the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. This conclusion is supported by the archived contingency, per‑episode validator traces, and reconciliation outputs.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. The bootstrap CI is degenerate because there are no discordant pairs to resample; every resample yields the same paired difference (0.0), producing zero empirical variance and CI [0.0,0.0]. This is an inferentially valid outcome and not an analysis error.

Ceiling‑effect contributors traceable in artifacts. The archived artifacts point to three concrete contributors: (1) task‑bank alignment—the task generator produced intents whose required_sequence and constraint structure closely matched the prompt schema and expected outputs, increasing syntactic correctness; (2) validator tightness—the deterministic validator encoded sequencing and precondition checks consistent with the synthesized reference answers so correct mappings passed validation readily (parsed_command_count == required_command_count in representative traces); and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model variance that could have produced discordant outcomes. Each contributor is traceable in the archived task manifest, model configuration, and per‑episode scoring traces.

Design recommendations. To enable nondegenerate measurement of verifier/gate value we recommend: (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates; (b) executing a design with independent generation per condition (two independent model calls per pair) or multiple samples per condition so guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model sampling variance are included in the estimand; (c) testing multiple model variants or sampling settings to reveal model variance effects; (d) increasing automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops to evaluate repair efficacy when initial violations occur; and (e) adding human‑in‑the‑loop arms to study operator decisions in response to validator flags. These recommendations follow directly from the archived execution accounting and manifest constraints (e.g., model_call budget implications and stage accounting).

Operational caveats. The null result does not imply deterministic validators lack value in adversarial or production regimes; rather it shows that the combination of task design, generation semantics, and validator rules determines whether a paired shared‑candidate contrast can detect verifier value. Field deployments require broader evaluation regimes (adversarial inputs, multiple draws, HITL arms) to quantify operational benefits and risks.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and no repairs were applied; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null outcome is specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the deterministic selection, the validator ruleset, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., independent per‑condition generation, adversarial inputs, multiple model samples) [1]–[3],[6]. We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions or vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicate the bank is dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
